incidents.victim: Rosstat (Russian Federal State Statistics Service)
incidents.vector: An unspecified intrusion disrupted Rosstat's IT systems; no attacker has publicly claimed responsibility or been confirmed in reporting reviewed.
incidents.impact: Russia's statistics agency failed to publish scheduled weekly price releases and other economic data on time, with delays expected to continue through at least Nov. 13, and some previously published data disappeared from its website.

incidents.victim: Italian government officials, including the foreign minister's office
incidents.vector: An unspecified cyberattack, attributed by Italian officials to pro-Russian hackers, compromised systems tied to the foreign minister's office.
incidents.impact: Confidential information concerning Italian government officials was reportedly offered for sale online; Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni linked the incident to a broader rise in hybrid disruptions from Russia-aligned actors.

incidents.victim: Financial-sector organizations in Southeast Asia and globally
incidents.vector: The actor, tracked by Microsoft as Storm-3358, combined the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX with conventional tools to scan the internet, exploit flaws such as anonymous file upload and SSRF, and install open-source remote access trojans.
incidents.impact: Compromised financial institutions faced automated brute-force and password-spraying attacks, API abuse, and database dumping conducted largely by AI agents, with the campaign expanding from a Southeast Asia focus to a smaller number of large global financial firms.

incidents.victim: Multiple companies across healthcare, finance, and technology sectors
incidents.attacker: Criminal gang — financial fraud using AI deepfakes
incidents.vector: Three men used AI-generated voice and video deepfakes to impersonate company CEOs and law-firm attorneys, directing lower-level employees to wire funds for purported confidential transactions.
incidents.impact: The scheme stole roughly $129 million between 2024 and 2026 from victims including a UK fintech, a Florida pet-food company, hospital systems in Missouri and California, a Massachusetts finance company, and a Rhode Island bank; all three men have been indicted and extradition is pending.

incidents.victim: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa
incidents.vector: An unspecified intrusion into the French banking group's systems enabled theft of funds, later traced through on-chain laundering activity.
incidents.impact: Hackers stole $133 million from the French banking group; blockchain investigators identified the theft this week after the stolen funds began moving through laundering channels.

incidents.victim: DigiCert
incidents.vector: An internal business system was inadvertently left externally accessible after a February 2025 network migration, allowing an unassigned account to be created and used to access a customer database starting June 27, 2026.
incidents.impact: Customer names, business emails, phone numbers, and identity documents such as driver's licenses and passports were exposed; DigiCert says certificate-issuance capability and login credentials were not affected.

incidents.victim: Chainstack
incidents.vector: An attacker used AI tools to speed up and automate an intrusion into the blockchain hosting platform's systems.
incidents.impact: Customer data was stolen from Chainstack in an incident that took place at the end of October.

incidents.victim: Federal Bureau of Investigation
incidents.attacker: Criminal — insider theft (former FBI supervisory special agent)
incidents.vector: A senior FBI Counterintelligence and Espionage Division official misused his authorized access to internal investigative systems to extract cryptocurrency wallet credentials tied to active cases.
incidents.impact: The agent stole more than $2.4 million in cryptocurrency across roughly 100 transfers from 79 wallets tied to 35 FBI investigations into nation-state hackers and crime victims, exposing investigative sources and methods before pleading guilty to wire fraud and money laundering.

incidents.victim: Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs
incidents.vector: Hackers breached the internal network of Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs in an intrusion that took place at the end of July 2026.
incidents.impact: The names and email addresses of 3,600 employees were stolen; the Ministry says the secure portion of its internal network was not affected.

incidents.victim: Norad (Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation)
incidents.vector: Hackers breached Norway's international aid agency via 27 compromised accounts.
incidents.impact: Personal data belonging to more than 20,000 grant applicants was stolen; Norad is working with Norway's National Security Authority to investigate.

incidents.victim: Perry Johnson Companies (medical transcription, coding, and imaging subsidiaries)
incidents.vector: An attacker used a stolen employee credential to access systems that lacked multi-factor authentication, then exfiltrated unencrypted files for roughly two months undetected.
incidents.impact: A March 2023 breach exposed the health data of more than 13 million people nationwide; the company agreed to pay $300,000 and overhaul its security practices to settle claims from four state attorneys general, with $9.7 million more due if it fails to make the required reforms.

incidents.victim: Executive Office of the President (White House)
incidents.vector: Several White House staffers installed residential-proxy apps on their devices that rent out the device's bandwidth to other users, with at least one app tied to a company that previously hosted malicious infrastructure.
incidents.impact: Staffer devices became part of third-party proxy networks, creating potential exposure of government network traffic and device activity to unknown operators.

incidents.victim: Li Auto electric vehicle owners in Russia
incidents.vector: Attackers took over master user accounts of Li Auto smart EVs, largely by exploiting Chinese eSIMs used to register the vehicles' master accounts.
incidents.impact: At least 20 confirmed owners — likely more — were locked out of their vehicles and extorted to regain control.

incidents.victim: Supermarket chains, cold-storage facilities, and blood banks across Europe
incidents.attacker: Unknown — pro-Kremlin hacktivist groups have claimed credit (unconfirmed)
incidents.vector: Attackers exploited internet-exposed, often default-credentialed Danfoss AK-SM/AK-SC, Copeland, and Dixell XWEB refrigeration controllers to force units into extended defrost cycles, reaching temperatures as high as 50°C (122°F).
incidents.impact: A first wave hit roughly 700 French supermarkets overnight Oct. 11-12; a second wave Nov. 1-2 spread to 10+ additional European countries and 100-115 more retail locations, spoiling food, damaging equipment, starting some fires, and briefly targeting French blood-bank refrigerators (no plasma losses confirmed); Ahold Delhaize alone expects up to €250 million in losses. CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT issued a joint advisory on the ongoing threat to industrial refrigeration and cold-chain systems.

incidents.victim: Owners of Android TV set-top boxes and other IoT devices worldwide
incidents.attacker: Criminal gang — ad fraud / proxy botnet operator (China-based manufacturer)
incidents.vector: Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co. intentionally built backdoor malware into Android TV set-top boxes, enrolling devices in a botnet dubbed XCPE that resold victims' internet connections through residential-proxy services.
incidents.impact: More than 1.3 million set-top boxes, plus over 10 million other compromised IoT devices (including telehealth devices and digital signage), were used for advertising fraud and proxy traffic until Google and industry partners dismantled the botnet's infrastructure.

incidents.victim: Cryptocurrency platforms including Flap, Kintsu, Pickle Finance, and Origami Finance
incidents.vector: A threat actor hijacked a customer-support account at domain registrar Name.com and redirected 15 cryptocurrency-related domains to phishing sites.
incidents.impact: Customer wallets connected to the affected platforms were drained after visitors were redirected to attacker-controlled phishing pages.

incidents.victim: The Kyiv Independent
incidents.vector: Russian-linked hackers breached the content management system of one of Ukraine's largest news agencies.
incidents.impact: The attackers sent a newsletter to subscribers containing fabricated claims, including that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had been shot and that he had launched a nuclear strike on Kyiv as a peace gesture toward Russia.

incidents.victim: Binance
incidents.vector: Hackers exploited an account-abstraction wallet permission feature on Ethereum (allowing an account to pre-authorize a contract to move funds) to drain assets across 11 cryptocurrencies, including one single transaction that moved 40% of the total haul for about $15 in gas fees.
incidents.impact: The attack stole $6.3 billion — the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, surpassing the $1.46 billion Bybit hack. Binance froze roughly $2.8 billion in stablecoins, leaving about $3.25 billion in unrecoverable Bitcoin and Ethereum; blockchain analysis firms and the FBI attributed the hack to a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor.

incidents.victim: Foreign ministries, pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, and telecommunications organizations across 14+ countries
incidents.vector: The actor used the agentic AI framework ARTEX, paired with the DeepSeek LLM and a second commercial LLM, to run parallel automated intrusions against more than 200 organizations, including building AI-driven evasion of endpoint security sensors into its workflow.
incidents.impact: Targets included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; a Middle East interior ministry; 19 U.S. organizations in pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors; and telecom providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines, with confirmed post-exploitation activity, including deployment of a custom backdoor, at nine organizations.

incidents.victim: Space and satellite services, defense/aerospace technology, and policy research organizations
incidents.vector: The actor exploited CVE-2026-20127, an authentication bypass flaw in Cisco SD-WAN Catalyst Controller instances, then installed a custom malware framework to intercept decrypted control-plane traffic and steal cryptographic keying material.
incidents.impact: The operation provided long-term persistent access for exfiltrating sensitive network keying material; Talos assesses the actor's infrastructure overlaps significantly with a known China-linked covert access network used for critical-infrastructure pre-positioning.

incidents.victim: A U.S. law firm
incidents.vector: China-nexus adversaries intensified operations against the legal sector: one actor exploited an ESXi zero-day for covert access, while another conducted large-scale password spraying against nearly 500 accounts at a single U.S. law firm from roughly 300 IP addresses over 30 days.
incidents.impact: CrowdStrike's 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report found China-nexus adversary diversity in the legal sector doubled year over year, with firms targeted for privileged client communications, M&A details, and intellectual property.
